candidates.label: scanning capacitance microscopy
candidates.definition: Microscopy which uses a small electrode to scan the surface of the specimen. An image of the surface is obtained by mechanically moving the probe in a raster scan of the specimen, line by line, and recording the electrostatic capacitance of the surface as a function of position. A feedback loop is used to maintain a fixed relationship between the electrode and surface during scanning.

candidates.label: constant-capacitance deep-level transient spectroscopy
candidates.definition: A method for determining the extent of intrinsic and process-induced defects in the  crystalline layers within  semiconductor devices. Defects arising from impurities, grain boundaries, interfaces, etc. result in the creation of traps that capture free electrons and holes. By holding the capacitance constant and monitoring the carrier emission produced when applying a voltage pulse to the semiconductor junction at different temperatures, spectra are generated which exhibit a peak for each 'deep level' (each energy level near the center of the band gap). The height of the peak is proportional to the defect density and the emission rate and temperature dependence are characteristic for each type of defect.

candidates.label: normalised isothermal capacitance transient spectroscopy
candidates.definition: A method for determining the extent of intrinsic and process-induced defects in the  crystalline layers within  semiconductor devices. Defects arising from impurities, grain boundaries, interfaces, etc. result in the creation of traps that capture free electrons and holes. By monitoring the normalised capacitance produced by applying a voltage pulse to the semiconductor junction at constant different temperatures, spectra are generated that exhibit peaks, the height of which are proportional to time constant for the emission rate.

candidates.label: differential isothermal capacitance transient spectroscopy
candidates.definition: A method for determining the extent of intrinsic and process-induced defects in the  crystalline layers within  semiconductor devices. Defects arising from impurities, grain boundaries, interfaces, etc. result in the creation of traps that capture free electrons and holes. By monitoring the differential of the capacitance produced by applying a voltage pulse to the semiconductor junction at constant different temperatures, spectra are generated that exhibit peaks, the height of which are proportional to the height of which are proportional to time constant for the emission rate.

candidates.label: E-type delayed fluorescence
candidates.definition: The process in which the first excited singlet state becomes populated by a thermally activated radiationless transition from the first excited triplet state. Since in this case the populations of the singlet and triplet states are in thermal equilibrium, the lifetimes of delayed fluorescence and the concomitant phosphorescence are equal.

candidates.label: E-type delayed luminescence

candidates.label: Solar E corona
candidates.definition: A part of the solar corona defined by the emission lines of hot gases. These emission lines include the so-called forbidden lines of the strongly ionized atoms of iron, calcium, and other elements. The E corona is thinner than the K corona and the F corona.

candidates.label: B(e) stars
candidates.definition: A Be star with forbidden lines in emission in its spectrum. B[e] stars show large infrared excess due to circumstellar dust emission.

candidates.label: E+A galaxies
candidates.definition: E+A galaxies have strong Balmer absorption lines typical of young stars, but lack optical emission features (e.g. O III 5007) typical of star-forming regions and have metallic absorption lines (e.g. Ca H and K) indicative of an older population of dwarf stars. The presence of two distinct stellar populations and morphological observations suggest that E+A galaxies are the product of a gas-rich galaxy merger.

candidates.label: E-folding time

candidates.label: Carbon dioxide
candidates.definition: CO_2, also called carbonic acid gas. A colorless gas which occurs in the atmosphere playing an essential part in animal respiration and the growth of green plants.  It is formed by the oxidation of carbon and carbon compounds. Carbon dioxide is the most important greenhouse gas produced by human activities, primarily through the combustion of fossil fuels. Its concentration in the Earth's atmosphere has risen by more than 30% since the Industrial Revolution. CO_2 forms a solid at -78.5 °C at atmospheric pressure, and is used as a refrigerant in this form as a dry ice for the preservation of frozen foods. As carbon dioxide gas is heavier than air and does not support combustion, it is used in fire extinguishers.  CO_2 is present in the interstellar medium and is one of the main molecules in comets.

 | Carbon dioxide is a colorless and odorless gas vital to life on Earth. This naturally occurring chemical compound is composed of a carbon atom covalently double bonded to two oxygen atoms. Carbon dioxide exists in Earth's atmosphere as a trace gas at a concentration of about 0.04 percent (400 ppm) by volume. Natural sources include volcanoes, hot springs and geysers, and it is freed from carbonate rocks by dissolution in water and acids. Because carbon dioxide is soluble in water, it occurs naturally in groundwater, rivers and lakes, in ice caps and glaciers and also in seawater. It is present in deposits of petroleum and natural gas.

candidates.definition: [Henderson's] CO2, a gas present in the atmosphere at a concentration of about 362 ppm. The main sources of atmospheric carbon dioxide are biological respiration, of which it is a waste product, combus­tion, and outgassing from the oceans. Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmo­sphere by photosynthesis and by solution in sea-water. Human activity has enhanced the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide by the burning of fossil fuels and biomass. It is a major greenhouse gas, trap­ping heat in the lower atmosphere.

candidates.definition: A colourless gas with a faint tingling smell and taste. Atmospheric carbon dioxide is the source of carbon for plants. As carbon dioxide is heavier than air and does not support combustion, it is used in fire extinguishers. It is a normal constituent of the atmosphere, relatively innocuous in itself but playing an important role in the greenhouse effect. It is produced during the combustion of fossil fuels when the carbon content of the fuels reacts with the oxygen during combustion. It is also produced when living organisms respire. It is essential for plant nutrition and in the ocean phytoplankton is capable of absorbing and releasing large quantities of the gas.

candidates.label: Carbon dioxide
candidates.definition: CO_2, also called carbonic acid gas. A colorless gas which occurs in the atmosphere playing an essential part in animal respiration and the growth of green plants.  It is formed by the oxidation of carbon and carbon compounds. Carbon dioxide is the most important greenhouse gas produced by human activities, primarily through the combustion of fossil fuels. Its concentration in the Earth's atmosphere has risen by more than 30% since the Industrial Revolution. CO_2 forms a solid at -78.5 °C at atmospheric pressure, and is used as a refrigerant in this form as a dry ice for the preservation of frozen foods. As carbon dioxide gas is heavier than air and does not support combustion, it is used in fire extinguishers.  CO_2 is present in the interstellar medium and is one of the main molecules in comets.

candidates.label: carbon nanotube based sensor
candidates.definition:
Carbon nanotubes (CNT) are rolled up seamless cylinders of graphene sheets, exhibiting many unique physical, mechanical and chemical properties.
CNT based biosensors are used to detect protein interactions, e.g. protein-DNA, antibody-aptamer interaction, etc.

candidates.label: carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A molecule consisting of a graphene cylinder or two or more concentric graphene cylinders.

candidates.label: single-walled carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A carbon nanotube consisting of a single graphene cylinder. Different kinds of single-walled carbon nanotube are distinguished by the indices (n,m) which describe the vector along which the graphene is rolled. The chiral angle is the angle between the vector and the origin and can take any value between 0 and 30°.

candidates.label: multi-walled carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A molecule consisting of three or more concentric graphene cylinders.

candidates.label: double-walled carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A carbon nanotube consisting of two concentric graphene cylinders.

candidates.label: armchair carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A single-walled carbon nanotube with equal n and m indices. Armchair carbon nanotubes have a chiral angle of 30° and are metallic.

candidates.label: zigzag carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A single walled carbon nanotube with (n,m) indices equal to (n,0) or (0,m). Zigzag carbon nanotubes have a chiral angle of 0° and can be either metallic or semiconducting.

candidates.label: chiral carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A single-walled carbon nanotube with unequal (n,m) indices and a chiral angle of between 0 and 30°.

candidates.label: metallic single-walled carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A single-walled carbon nanotube with (n,m) indices such that n−m is a multiple of 3.

candidates.label: semiconducting single-walled carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A single-walled carbon nanotube with (n,m) indices such that n−m is not a multiple of 3.

candidates.label: carbon nanorod
candidates.definition: A nanostructure produced by filling the hollow cavity of a carbon nanotube with different substance.

candidates.label: nitrogen-doped carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: A carbon nanotube grown in a nitrogen-rich atmosphere, in which a small percentage of carbon atoms have been replaced by nitrogen atoms.

candidates.label: boron-doped carbon nanotube
candidates.definition: Carbon nanotubes grown in a boron-rich atmosphere, in which a small percentage of carbon atoms have been replaced by boron atoms.

candidates.label: boron-carbon-nitrogen nanotube
candidates.definition: A carbon nanotube grown in a boron- and nitrogen-rich atmosphere in which some of the carbon atoms have been replaced by B and N atoms in the order C > B > N.

candidates.label: carbon nanorope
candidates.definition: A carbon nanostructure consisting of carbon nanotubes which have been spun or bundled together.

candidates.label: carbon nanotube column
candidates.definition: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are known to have high thermal and mechanical stability and have the potential to be high-performance separation media that utilize the nanoscale interactions. CNT can be applied in long capillary tubes for the development of gas chromatography columns. A film of CNTs can be deposited by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) to form the stationary phase in the open tubular format. Altering the CVD conditions can vary the thickness and the morphology of the CNT film, which opens the possibility of selectivity tuning. The ability to fabricate long tubes coated with CNTs can be readily employed in other gas- and liquid-phase separations as well.

candidates.label: B stars
candidates.definition: A star of spectral type B, whose spectrum is marked by absorption lines of hydrogen; also known as B-type star. B-type optical spectra are characterized by the presence of neutral He lines (mainly He I 4471 Å) at about type B9. He I strengthens up to about B2, then decreases. Ionized helium (mainly He II 4541 Å) first appears at about B0. Most metallic lines are absent or weak, except some absorption lines for the higher ionization states of silicon, oxygen, carbon, and magnesium. These are hot stars with effective temperatures ranging from about 10,000 K at B9 to nearly 30,000 K at B0. They are between 3 and 20 solar masses. Some famous examples include  Rigel, Achernar, and Hadar.

candidates.label: hydrogen gas electrode
candidates.definition: A reference gas electrode based on the equilibrium between aqueous protons and electrons on one side and hydrogen gas on the other, in solutions saturated with hydrogen gas. Typically it is made of "a thin foil of platinum electrolytically coated with a finely divided deposit of platinum or palladium metal".

candidates.label: pH glass electrode
candidates.definition: "A hydrogen-ion responsive electrode usually consisting of a bulb, or other suitable form, of special glass attached to a stem of high resistance glass complete with internal reference electrode and internal filling solution system."

candidates.label: silver/silver chloride reference electrode
candidates.definition: A reference electrode where the electrochemical reaction is between silver metal and silver(I) chloride.

candidates.label: saturated calomel electrode
candidates.definition: A reference electrode where the electrochemical reaction is between mercury metal and mercury(I) chloride.

candidates.label: auxiliary electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode that "serves merely to carry the current flowing through the cell, and at the surface of which no processes of interest occur."

candidates.label: ion-selective electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode which responds to the activity of a primary ion in presence of various other (interfering) ions in the sample solution. Ion-selective electrodes contain a selective membrane which contains fixed or mobile sites that interact with ions in solution.

candidates.label: dropping mercury electrode
candidates.definition: An "electrode formed by a sequence of mercury drops falling from a small aperture."

candidates.label: hanging mercury drop electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode formed of a partial mercury drop of controlled geometry and surface area at the end of a capillary.

candidates.label: quasi-reference electrode
candidates.definition: A reference electrode that is based on a ferrocene or cobaltocene redox couple internal standard.

candidates.label: pseudo-reference electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode through which no appreciable current is allowed to flow and is used to observe or control the potential at a working electrode. A pseudo-reference electrode, such as a Ag wire, fulfils the role of a reference electrode but the electrochemical processes allowing it to do so are not well understood, in contrast to a true reference electrode.

candidates.label: interrogating electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode whose response indicates the change of some analytical variable.

candidates.label: saturated mercury sulfate electrode
candidates.definition: A reference electrode where the electrochemical reaction is between mercury metal and mercury(II) sulfate.

candidates.label: carbon electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode that "comprises granular carbon material bound with pitch" and has been fired at high temperature.

candidates.label: graphite electrode
candidates.definition: A carbon electrode that has been "fired at a temperature around 2800 K", resulting in a largely graphitic composition.

candidates.label: rotating-disk electrode
candidates.definition: An indicator electrode that usually consists of a Pt disc (diameter 1.0 mm) sealed in a Teflon carrier which rotates a high speed during the experiment. Rotating-disk electrodes are used to investigate reaction mechanisms.

candidates.label: scanning vibrating electrode technique
candidates.definition: A technique that operates by mechanically vibrating a probe at a fixed amplitude, frequency and height over an electrochemically active sample in solution measuring and mapping the electric field generated by the sample. This technique is used to probe the nature of corrosion processes.

candidates.label: glass-like carbon electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode consisting of agranular non-graphitizable carbon with high isotropy and low permeability for liquids and gases.

candidates.label: micro electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode of very fine caliber consisting usually of a fine wire or a glass tube of capillary diameter drawn to a fine point and filled with saline or a metal used in physiological experiments to stimulate or record action currents of extracellular or intracellular origin in the nervous system.

candidates.label: electrode puller
candidates.definition: A device used in the first step in making electrodes, that applies constant tension on a glass capillary tube and eventually breaks it while heating it; this produces a very fine point on the capillary tube.

candidates.label: two electrode voltage clamp assay
candidates.definition: The two electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) method utilizes two low-resistance pipettes, one sensing voltage and the other injecting current. The microelectrodes are filled with conductive solution and inserted into the cell to artificially control membrane potential. The membrane acts as a dielectric as well as a resistor, while the fluids on either side of the membrane function as capacitors.[9] The microelectrodes compare the membrane potential against a command voltage, giving an accurate reproduction of the currents flowing across the membrane. Current readings can be used to analyze the electrical response of the cell to different applications. This technique is mainly used in the Oocyte preparation.

candidates.label: local field potential recording
candidates.definition: An extracellular electrophysiology assay where a microelectrode is placed in the extracellular space of brain tissue to measure action potential and compared to an electrode either outside or inside that tissue.

candidates.label: multi-electrode array plate
candidates.definition: A measurement device consisting of grid of tightly spaced microscopic electrodes that can detect the electrical signals of cells in close proximity.

candidates.label: multi-electrode array assay
candidates.definition: A multi-unit recording assay using a multi-electrode array (MEA) on the surface of a well on a cell culture plate.

candidates.label: count of multi-electrode plate electrodes detecting action potential assay
candidates.definition: A multi-electrode array assay that measures the number of electrodes in a well where the mean rate of action potentials is at least 5 spikes per minute.

candidates.label: count of multi-electrode plate electrodes detecting neuron burst assay
candidates.definition: A multi-electrode array assay that measures the number of electrodes in a well where the burst rate is at least 0.5 bursts per minute.

candidates.label: count of multi-electrode plate electrodes detecting spike peak assay
candidates.definition: A multi-electrode array assay that measures the average number of electrodes detecting a network spike, measured at the peak of a network spike.

candidates.label: electrode process
candidates.definition: The totality of changes occurring at or near a single electrode during the passage of current.

candidates.label: electrode reaction
candidates.definition: For an electrode process at a given potential the current is controlled by the kinetics of a number of steps which include the transport of reactants to and from the interface and the interfacial reaction itself. The latter, which is called the electrode reaction, must always include at least one elementary step in which charge is transferred from one phase to the other, but may also involve purely chemical steps within the interfacial region.

candidates.label: electrodeposition
candidates.definition: The deposition of dissolved or suspended material by an electric field on an electrode.

candidates.label: electrode
candidates.definition: The two electronically conducting parts of an electrochemical cell.

candidates.label: working electrode
candidates.definition: The electrode in a three-electrode cell where "the action is".

candidates.label: counter electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode in a three-electrode cell that is used only to make an electrical connection to the electrolyte so that a current can be applied to the working electrode.

candidates.label: reference electrode
candidates.definition: An electrode that has a well known and stable equilibrium electrode potential.

candidates.label: scan rate potential
candidates.definition: In cyclic voltammetry, the rate at which the potential of the working electrode is varied, i.e., = (dE/dt). The value of is always cited as positive.

candidates.label: reversible hydrogen electrode
candidates.definition: A commonly used reference electrode. A hydrogen electrode immersed directly into the electrolyte of the electrochemical cell and usually (unless otherwise stated) operated with one atmosphere pressure hydrogen gas. The equilibrium potential depends on the hydrogen ion concentration (strictly speaking, activity) of the cell electrolyte.

candidates.label: rotating-disk electrode
candidates.definition: A specialized hydrodynamic electrode used in the study of the kinetics and mechanism of electrode reactions and in electroanalysis for ensuring a known and controllable flow of solution over the electrode.

candidates.label: (RC,RS)-sulfoxaflor
candidates.definition: A [methyl(oxido){1-[6-(trifluoromethyl)pyridin-3-yl]ethyl}-λ6-sulfanylidene]cyanamide that has R configuration at both the sulfur atom and at the carbon attached to position 3 of the pyridine ring.

candidates.label: (RC,SS)-sulfoxaflor
candidates.definition: A [methyl(oxido){1-[6-(trifluoromethyl)pyridin-3-yl]ethyl}-λ6-sulfanylidene]cyanamide that has S configuration at the sulfur atom and R configuration at the carbon attached to position 3 of the pyridine ring.

candidates.label: ginsenoside Rc
candidates.definition: A ginsenoside found in Panax ginseng that is dammarane which is substituted by hydroxy groups at the 3β, 12β and 20 pro-S positions, in which the hydroxy groups at positions 3 and 20 have been converted to the corresponding β-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→2)-β-D-glucopyranoside and α-L-arabinofuranosyl-(1→6)-β-D-glucopyranoside respectively, and in which a double bond has been introduced at the 24-25 position.

candidates.label: cathodic stripping potentiometry
candidates.definition: An electrochemical technique where the analyte of interest is electroplated onto the working electrode before being removed or 'stripped' by re-reduction. During removal the time-dependence of the potential difference between the indicator and reference electrodes is measured under conditions where the current passed is sufficiently small to maintain thermodynamic equilibrium.

candidates.label: cathodic stripping voltammetry
candidates.definition: A stripping voltammetry in which the analyte of interest is first electroplated onto the working electrode before being removed or 'stripped' by applying a reducing potential.

candidates.label: StrippingVoltammetry
candidates.definition: Two-step electrochemical measurement in which 1) material is accumulated at an electrode and 2) the amount of an accumulated species is measured by voltammetry. The measured electric current in step 2 is related to the concentration of analyte in the solution by calibration. Anodic stripping voltammetry (ASV) was historically used to measure concentrations of metal ions in solution using cathodic accumulation with mercury to form an amalgam. Due to the toxicity of mercury and its compounds, inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry have frequently replaced ASV at mercury electrodes in the laboratory, often sacrificing the probing of speciation and lability in complex matrices. Mercury has now been replaced by non-toxic bismuth or anti- mony as films on a solid electrode support (such as glassy carbon) with equally good sensi- tivity and detection limits. Because the accumulation (pre-concentration) step can be prolonged, increasing the amount of material at the electrode, stripping voltammetry is able to measure very small concentrations of analyte. Often the product of the electrochemical stripping is identical to the analyte before the accumulation. Stripping voltammetry is a calibrated method to establish the relation between amount accumulated in a given time and the concentration of the analyte in solution. Types of stripping voltammetry refer to the kind of accumulation (e.g. adsorptive stripping voltammetry) or the polarity of the stripping electrochemistry (anodic, cathodic stripping voltammetry).

candidates.label: cathodic stripping potentiometry
candidates.definition: An electrochemical technique where the analyte of interest is electroplated onto the working electrode before being removed or 'stripped' by re-reduction. During removal the time-dependence of the potential difference between the indicator and reference electrodes is measured under conditions where the current passed is sufficiently small to maintain thermodynamic equilibrium.

candidates.definition: A stripping voltammetry in which the analyte of interest is first electroplated onto the working electrode before being removed or 'stripped' by applying a reducing potential.

candidates.label: active geological fault
candidates.definition: An active fault is a fault that is likely to become the source of another earthquake sometime in the future. Geologists commonly consider faults to be active if there has been movement observed or evidence of seismic activity during the last 10,000 years.

candidates.label: geothermally active field
candidates.definition: A field in which geothermal processes occur.

candidates.label: photosynthetically active radiation
candidates.definition: Electromagnetic radidation which involves radiant energy in a spectral range (wave band) between 400 to 700 nanometers, that photosynthetic organisms are able to use in the process of photosynthesis.

candidates.label: active permafrost layer
candidates.definition: A layer which is composed of ground that is 1) subject to annual thawing and freezing and 2) present in areas underlain by permafrost.

candidates.label: active transport
candidates.definition: The carriage of a solute across a biological membrane from low to high concentration which requires the expenditure of (metabolic) energy.

candidates.label: Area
candidates.definition: A subclass of s4bldg:BuildingSpace used to define the physical spaces of the building. According to IEC 62264, areas are physical, geographical or logical groupings of resources determined by the site. A site can be divided in areas, whereas areas contain work centers.s.

candidates.label: area
candidates.definition: area is a quantity that pertains to the extent of a two-dimensional surface or shape, or planar lamina, in the plane.

candidates.label: active movement
candidates.definition: active movement is the process in which an object is spatially displaced using some chemical energy.

candidates.label: primary active transport
candidates.definition: primary active transport, also called direct active transport, directly uses energy to transport molecules across a membrane.

candidates.label: secondary active transport
candidates.definition: secondary active transport or co-transport uses electrochemical potential difference created by pumping ions out of the cell to transport molecules across a membrane.

candidates.label: active site
candidates.definition: An active site is a molecular site in which a chemical event occurs (structural transformation or conformational change).

candidates.label: active ingredient
candidates.definition: An active ingredient is a molecular entity that exhibits biological activity.

candidates.label: active transport
candidates.definition: active transport is the movement of a substance across a membrane against its concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and requires chemical energy.

candidates.label: active area
candidates.definition: the area of a photovoltaic device which is active in the conversion of light to current

candidates.label: Active galactic nuclei
candidates.definition: A central region of an active galaxy, which is a light-year or less in diameter and has an abnormally high luminosity. The nucleus emits high energy radiation (gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet) and shows variability over various time-scales, sometimes very short (hours to weeks). Emission line spectra reveal high velocity motions up to 10^4 km s^-1. AGNs are divided into two main types. Type I refers to an AGN whose nucleus is visible (the spectra has both narrow and broad emission lines), while in type II AGN, the broad line region (BLR) is obscured and the lines are very narrow. This may be due either to the viewing angle or some intrinsic difference in structure.

candidates.label: Active galaxies
candidates.definition: A galaxy that produces huge amounts of energy at its center, which cannot be attributed to normal processes from stars, interstellar medium, and their interactions. There are several types of active galaxies: Seyfert galaxies, quasars, and blazars. All of these objects show brightness variations, some as short as 3 hours. These fluctuations indicate a relatively very small size for the central object, because an object cannot vary in brightness faster than light can travel across it. For example, an object that is one light-year in diameter cannot vary significantly in brightness over a period of less than one year.

candidates.label: Active sun
candidates.definition: The Sun during its 11-year cycle of activity when spots, flares, prominences, and variations in radiofrequency radiation are at a maximum.

candidates.label: active site
candidates.definition: Those sites for adsorption which are the effective sites for a particular heterogeneous catalytic reaction.

candidates.label: active acquisition time
candidates.definition: The net time during which the detector is actively recording, excluding time lost to processing (dead time).

candidates.label: active area
candidates.definition: In contrast to substrate area, the actual area of a sample or electrode which is active.

candidates.label: inlet gas pressure
candidates.definition: An inlet gas pressure is a quality qualification facet that quantifies the pressure of the inlet gas. [Allotrope]

candidates.label: collision gas pressure
candidates.definition: The gas pressure of the collision gas used for collisional excitation.

candidates.label: Pressure increase
candidates.definition:
Measuring the time until reaching a  certain permeate pressure during a gas permeability measurement on a membrane. For a single experiment, the feed pressure is set at the beginning and decreases over time due to permeatation.
(https://doi.org/10.3390/membranes9020022)

candidates.label: cell seeding density
candidates.definition: Cell seeding density is a measurement datum which denotes the number of cells per surface area in the case of adherent cells or number of cells per volume in the case of free cells deposited in the culture vessel to start a cell culture. The cell seeding density is therefore stated in number of cells per cm2 or number of cells per ml.

candidates.label: reddening (U-B)
candidates.definition: Reddening measured with the U and B passbands.

candidates.label: U magnitude
candidates.definition: Johnson U magnitude. The Johnson U band is a standard passband in the ultraviolet area. The central wavelength is 365nm and the bandwidth is 70nm.  The filter to be used is the Corning 9863 filter.

candidates.label: u magnitude
candidates.definition: u Magnitude in the Strömgren photometric system with a peak wavelength at 350 nm and a peak-half-width of 30 nm.

candidates.label: open circuit voltage
candidates.definition: The cell voltage under zero current conditions.

candidates.label: Board Voltage Sensor
candidates.definition: Sensor used to measure board input voltage.

candidates.label: centrifugal evaporation
candidates.definition: The evaporation of solvent from a sample by placing it a centrifuge and spinning it rapidly.

candidates.label: analytical centrifugation
candidates.definition: A separation method where components of a sample are separated on the basis of their density in a centrifuge according to the centrifugal force they experience. During centrifugation the sample can be monitored in real time through an optical detection system or using ultraviolet light absorption.

candidates.label: sequential centrifugation
candidates.definition: A separation method where the components of a sample are separated on the basis of their density in a centrifuge according to the centrifugal force they experience. The sample is centrifuged in a number of separate, sequential steps.

candidates.label: low-speed centrifugation
candidates.definition: A separation method where the components of a sample  are separated on the basis of their density in a centrifuge according to the centrifugal force they experience. Samples are spun at <5000 rpm.

candidates.label: high-speed centrifugation
candidates.definition: A separation method where components of a sample are separated on the basis of their density in a centrifuge according to the centrifugal force they experience. Samples are spun at >5000 rpm.

candidates.label: preparative centrifugation
candidates.definition: A method where a sample is purified by removing impurities on the basis of their density in a centrifuge.

candidates.label: differential centrifugation
candidates.definition: A separation method where the components of a cell are separated on the basis of their density in a centrifuge according to the centrifugal force they experience. The sample is centrifuged in a number of separate, sequential steps; each time the pellet is removed and the speed increased.

candidates.label: density-gradient centrifugation
candidates.definition: A method where the components of a sample are separated on the basis of their density, in a dense medium or density gradient, in a centrifuge, according to the centrifugal force they experience.

candidates.label: isopycnic centrifugation
candidates.definition: A method where the components of a sample are separated on the basis of their density, in a density gradient of e.g. CsCl in a centrifuge, according to buoyant density. The species in the sample move through the gradient until they reach a point where their density and that of the gradient are identical.

candidates.label: rate-zonal centrifugation
candidates.definition: A method where the components of a sample are separated on the basis of their density, in a density gradient of e.g. CsCl in a centrifuge, according to mass. candidates.label: CyclicVoltammetry
candidates.definition: Voltammetry in which the electric current is recorded as the electrode potential is varied with time cyclically between two potential limits, normally at a constant scan rate. Cyclic voltammetry is frequently used for the investigation of mechanisms of electrochemical/electrode reactions. The current-potential curve may be modelled to obtain reaction mechanisms and electrochemical parameters. Normally the initial potential is chosen where no electrode reaction occurs and the switching potential is greater (more positive for an oxidation or more negative for a reduction) than the peak potential of the analyte reaction. The initial potential is usually the negative or positive limit of the cycle but can have any value between the two limits, as can the initial scan direction. The limits of the potential are known as the switching potentials. The plot of current against potential is termed a cyclic voltammogram. Usually peak-shaped responses are obtained for scans in both directions.
